agent_response.summary: Candidate 3 changes one value from candidate 2: the frequency chunk size goes from 1 to 2. The loop now runs 51 blocks of two frequencies. Frequency 101 is duplicated once as padding and the duplicate is thrown away. Candidate 2 (aa7c3f93) passed the official check and failed strict, with the same failure as candidate 1. Its full run took 21.798 s (parent 24.657). Forward execution took 9.05 s, gradient execution 0.70 s, warm median 10.07 s, peak RSS 7.31 GB. All physical outputs matched exactly. Gradient index 161 (boundary01.power) failed with a value identical to candidate 1's to within about 1e-14. That rules out the carrier accumulation-order explanation.
agent_response.hypothesis: Candidates 1 and 2 match the forward outputs bit for bit, but their whole gradient differs from baseline at about 9e-10 relative L2, where the parent was at about 1e-17. So the difference comes from operations that only run in the reverse pass. My leading guess, unverified, is that with k=1 every inner batch dimension has size 1. XLA simplifies such dimensions away, which picks different dot and triangular-solve kernels for the reverse pass than the batched parent uses. With k=2 the batch dimension is real, which should bring back the parent's batched kernels and strict agreement on index 161. Blocks of two should keep most of the memory and cache benefit, at about 1% extra solve work from the padding. Expected: forward slightly above 9.0 s and RSS slightly above 7.3 GB.
agent_response.notes: The notes file has run IDs, phase times, memory, comparisons and the rejected hypothesis for candidate 2. Index 161 is a small gradient entry (−29.6, against a gradient norm of 7e4) that comes out of heavy cancellation, so it amplifies any change in rounding. Candidates 1 and 2 are official-only results with strong timing gains (about −2.6 to −2.9 s first run, −42% RSS, single runs). If k=2 passes strict, it becomes the first validated value of the operator; then try 4 or 8 for timing. If k=2 still fails at the same size, then any change in batching granularity changes the reverse-pass rounding. In that case I'll document the operator as qualifying only for the official check at the tested values and hand off.
